conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected ~30 us lower per-call floor on the 9 launch-bound workloads; observed only 75.0 -> 67.2 us (timing-0), 79.4 -> 65.8 (timing-2), 86.0 -> 66.4 (timing-10) and essentially unchanged 4096x4096 cases (0.604/0.601/0.604 ms), giving geo_mean 0.13037 -> 0.12965, i.e. no gain. plan.code_changes: Added _fast_launch(): it reuses triton's own device_caches/binder/compute_cache_key so the exact same specialization key (dtype, pointer alignment, divisibility) still selects the same compiled binary, then calls the cached CompiledKernel.run directly (grid, stream, function, packed_metadata, bound args) instead of JITFunction.run. On the first call for a specialization it returns False so the caller performs the stock literal kernel[grid](...) launch (single execution, compiles and caches); any exception permanently falls back to the stock path. Kernels, BLOCK_SIZE=1024, math and the strided path are unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: The dominant cost is host dispatch, not device work: measured per-call host submission is ~55 us for the triton JIT path versus ~30 us for a cached compiled-kernel launch and 7.5 us for torch.selu_. Bypassing JITFunction.run while keeping triton's specialization key should cut ~30 us from every workload whose kernel is only a few microseconds, leaving the 4096x4096 workloads (device bound) unchanged.

expected_effect.mechanism: Removing triton's per-call option/hook/binding re-work drops host submission from ~55 us to ~30 us, which is the entire floor of the 1024/65536-element workloads and most of the 1048576-element ones

key_params.launch_path: cached CompiledKernel.run with triton specialization key

conclusion.root_cause: The intended launch-path bypass never took effect. JITFunction.run sets kwargs['debug'] and calls _flagprism.apply_compile_options(kwargs) before binder(), so the options that feed compute_cache_key differ from the ones obtained by my bare binder(x, n, BLOCK_SIZE=1024) call; the recomputed key therefore missed on every invocation. _fast_launch returned False each time and the caller executed the stock literal kernel[grid](...) launch, so round 2 was functionally identical to round 1 (same 66-69 us host floor, exact numerics).
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: Expected ~30 us lower per-call floor on the 9 launch-bound workloads; observed only 75.0 -> 67.2 us (timing-0), 79.4 -> 65.8 (timing-2), 86.0 -> 66.4 (timing-10) and essentially unchanged 4096x4096 cases (0.604/0.601/0.604 ms), giving geo_mean 0.13037 -> 0.12965, i.e. no gain. The gap is fully explained by the fast path never launching: the in-process probe shows _SLOW remained False, the recomputed key's kernel_cache.get() returned None (compiled_type NoneType), so every call still ran the stock JIT launch at ~69 us/call in batch mode, matching the observed eval floor. Reference latencies also moved between rounds (11.6 -> 8.2-10.4 us on the small workloads), so the small delta is within environment noise rather than a real effect.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Key the cached launch on triton's own `specialization` list returned by binder (which is independent of the injected options) plus BLOCK_SIZE, and capture the compiled handle by diffing kernel_cache keys before/after the stock launch instead of recomputing the option-dependent cache key. Also use x.device.index instead of get_current_device. Re-verify on the target that the fast path actually launches (compiled handle found) and that one call performs exactly one kernel execution.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A cached compiled-kernel fast path must be validated in-process: assert that the lookup actually hits (here kernel_cache.get(key) was None on every call) instead of inferring engagement from the measured latency alone. Recomputing triton's cache key from binder() alone is invalid because run() injects FlagPrism compile options and debug into the options before binding.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 1 showed host dispatch dominates 9 of 12 timing workloads; round 2 attempted a cached compiled-kernel launch but silently fell back to the JIT path due to a cache-key mismatch. (1) Nine of the twelve timing workloads are host-launch bound: profiled device task duration for selu_-timing-0 (fp16 [1024]) is 1.65 us against a 13.16 us walltime, and a target-side host-cost probe measured the candidate's per-call host path at 12.17 us versus 11.5 us for the PyTorch reference wrapper shape and 9.2 us for the bare compiled-launcher floor. plan.strategy: Narrow the bf16 math width so the bf16 tile can double, halving its MTE transfer count.
plan.code_changes: _selu_nomask/_selu_masked gain an explicit bfloat16 branch that casts the loaded tile to float16, runs the same fp16-width expression, and rounds the result back to bfloat16; _pick_block now caps BLOCK at 8192 only for float32 (16384 for fp16 and bf16). fp32 path, strided kernel, host dispatch and profiler gate unchanged.
plan.hypothesis: bf16 runs fp32-domain math, whose three live full-width UB tiles cap BLOCK at 8192 and therefore double the MTE transfer count; doing the math at fp16 width fits BLOCK 16384. Target probe at n=16777216: 83.82 us for the current bf16 form versus 64.45 us for the fp16-width form, with 0 of 16777216 elements outside the bf16 tolerance (max abs error 0.0175).

expected_effect.mechanism: Halving the bf16 program count halves the MTE transfers (2048 -> 1024 for 16.7M elements), which is the cost driver measured on this target.

conclusion.root_cause: The bf16 root cause is confirmed and was fixed as predicted: bf16 was running fp32-domain math, which needs three live full-width UB tiles and therefore caps BLOCK at 8192, doubling the MTE transfer count relative to fp16 at BLOCK 16384; the fp16-width bf16 branch compiles at 16384 and delivers the predicted 63.5 us. The aggregate regression has a different, unrelated cause: bilateral machine-level drift of about 12% on the host-bound small workloads between the round-2 and round-3 measurements, which the retest quantified and which no code change in this round could have produced.
conclusion.perf_gap_analysis: The frozen expectation was that halving the bf16 transfer count would move selu_-timing-7 from 0.71 toward 0.90, and the workload-level evidence matched exactly: 83.310 -> 63.477 us, speedup 0.710 -> 0.932, versus the 64.45 us that the pre-round target probe predicted, with correctness unchanged (0 bad elements; bf16 correctness cases still 1.0 matched ratio, max rel err 0.044). The aggregate nevertheless fell from 0.8839 to 0.8670 because the nine small workloads, whose kernels and host path are byte-identical to round 2 and which this change cannot affect, all moved +1.5 to +2.0 us together with their own reference latencies. A full-suite retest confirmed the drift was bilateral and not the candidate: reference latencies returned to 10.46-11.75 us (from 11.94-13.30) and candidate latencies to 11.64-13.66 us, giving a remeasured geo_mean of 0.8727 with timing-7 (63.472 us) and timing-11 (82.682 us) unchanged within 0.1%. So the device change delivered its predicted 31% on timing-7, while the headline metric moved the opposite way purely through measurement drift on the host-bound majority; the round is not an improvement on the ledger even though its kernel is strictly better on the one workload it targets.
conclusion.next_suggestion: Re-establish the verified bf16 narrowing (it is a real 83.3 -> 63.5 us device win on selu_-timing-7 and has no effect on any other dtype, since the bf16 branch is compile-time eliminated elsewhere) and, in the same submission, recover the remaining host-side slack measured on target by dropping the extra Python frame and the unused tensor argument on the launcher call, then verify the combined form under the retest path if the two sides drift again.
conclusion.debug_lesson: A geo_mean comparison across rounds on this shared card is only meaningful if both sides moved together: here the reference latencies for the nine small workloads swung 11.7 -> 12.5 -> 11.2 us mean across three measurements of the same code, which is larger than any host-path change made so far. Round-to-round comparisons therefore need the retest path or a per-workload device-task measurement before concluding that a candidate regressed.
conclusion.strategy_evolution: Round 2 exhausted the host-launch lever; round 3 moved to the device/transfer-count regime and its mechanism was verified per workload, but the ledger decision is dominated by drift on the other twelve-twelfths of the suite. Strategy changes accordingly: subsequent rounds must pair a verified device win with same-state verification (retest) rather than trusting a single cross-round aggregate.
